title: Attention-fragment kernel predictor with NCCL interleaver for multi-GPU prefill/decode
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: We need an integrated runtime component that predicts per-token kernel choices and fragments attention work such that communication (NCCL) can be interleaved with compute across heterogeneous GPU fleets during prefill and decode. Goal is to reduce 95th percentile latency for multi-GPU prefill/decode flows by 15-30% while maintaining or improving throughput and avoiding model-output regressions.

Background and problem: Current multi-GPU prefill/decode pipelines frequently hit serialization points where large attention and KV cache ops block NCCL all-reduce/all-gather windows, causing tail latency spikes on heterogeneous racks. Kernel selection is currently static per-model/sequence-length bucket which misses runtime variance due to attention sparsity, prompt length skew, and device bandwidth differences.

Proposed approach: 1) Attention fragmentation: break large attention and KV tasks into smaller fragments (logical attention slabs) that preserve correctness but can be scheduled interleaved with communication. Fragments sized based on observed token wavefronts and device memory pressure. 2) Kernel predictor: lightweight online model (small decision tree / logistic regression with features: sequence length, active KV size, sparsity estimate from first-layer attention diagnostics, device_bandwidth_estimate, historic kernel latency) to choose among a small set of kernels (fused-attention, split-attention, quantized-path). Predictor runs per-request at prefill and adjusts for decode routing. 3) NCCL interleaver: runtime reorderer that exposes comm ops at fragment boundaries and schedules them across GPUs to maximize overlap with compute on other devices; includes backpressure hooks and adaptive window sizing. 4) Graceful fallback: if predictor confidence low or fragmentation causes memory pressure, fall back to conservative contiguous attention path.

Design trade-offs: - Fragmentation reduces atomic compute efficiency (smaller GEMM windows) but enables comm overlap; we must tune fragment size for each model and hardware. - Online predictor complexity: heavier models give better accuracy but add CPU overhead and complexity; start with simple heuristic/linear model and add richer features only if necessary. - NCCL semantics: reordering must preserve algorithmic correctness; interleaver only operates at fragment-level consistent with model graph.

Acceptance criteria: - End-to-end 95th pct latency reduction of >=15% on heterogeneous racks (mix of A100 and A10x) for representative prefill+decode workloads (bench suite attached). - No degradation in output quality measured by existing eval suites (ROUGE/LLM-eval sets) beyond noise. - CPU overhead added by predictor < 2% of request CPU budget in p99. - Canary rollout plan with automated rollback on error rate or latency regressions.

Observability and telemetry: new metrics: fragment_count, fragment_size_histogram, predictor_choice, predictor_confidence, nccL_overlap_ratio, comm_wait_ms_per_gpu. Dashboards: per-model fragment profile, cross-GPU overlap heatmap. Tracing: tag spans for fragment boundaries and NCCL windows.

Testing plan: - Unit tests for fragmentation correctness and fallback paths. - Synthetic microbenchmarks: sequence-length sweep, sparsity sweep, device bandwidth throttling. - Staging canary: 5% traffic on runtime-1.19 with canary gating thresholds: p95 latency +5% allowed, error-rate < 0.1%.

Rollout: feature-flag controlled; start with a single model family (gpt-small family) on a heterogeneous dedicated pool. Monitor for 48h then expand to more models.

Links: design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUN/Attn+Fragmentation+Design; benchmark sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/benchmark-attn-frag; experimental PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1789
